arXiv:2602.16570v1 [cs.LG] 18 Feb 2026

Steering diffusion models with quadratic rewards:
a fine-grained analysis

Abstract

Inference-time algorithms are an emerging paradigm in which pre-trained models are used as subroutines to solve downstream tasks. Such algorithms have been proposed for tasks ranging from inverse problems and guided image generation to reasoning. However, the methods currently deployed in practice are heuristics with a variety of failure modes—and we have very little understanding of when these heuristics can be efficiently improved.

In this paper, we consider the task of sampling from a reward-tilted diffusion model—that is, sampling from p⋆​(x)∝p⁡(x)​exp⁡(𝐫⁡(x))p^{\star}(x)\propto p(x)\exp(\mathbf{r}(x))—given a reward function 𝐫\mathbf{r} and pre-trained diffusion oracle for pp. We provide a fine-grained analysis of the computational tractability of this task for quadratic rewards 𝐫⁡(x)=x⊤​A​x+b⊤​x\mathbf{r}(x)=x^{\top}Ax+b^{\top}x. We show that linear-reward tilts are always efficiently sampleable—a simple result that seems to have gone unnoticed in the literature. We use this as a building block, along with a conceptually new ingredient—the Hubbard-Stratonovich transform—to provide an efficient algorithm for sampling from low-rank positive-definite quadratic tilts, i.e. 𝐫⁡(x)=x⊤​A​x\mathbf{r}(x)=x^{\top}Ax where AA is positive-definite and of rank O⁡(1)O(1). For negative-definite tilts, i.e. 𝐫⁡(x)=−x⊤​A​x\mathbf{r}(x)=-x^{\top}Ax where AA is positive-definite, we prove that the problem is intractable even if AA is of rank 1 (albeit with exponentially-large entries).

1 Introduction

It is increasingly common to use pre-trained generative models as components within algorithms for more complex downstream tasks. Broadly, such algorithms are termed as inference-time or meta-generation algorithms (Welleck et al., 2024). Examples of tasks that can be framed in this paradigm include inverse problems in the sciences (Bruna and Han, 2024), guidance to perform conditional sampling in image generation (Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021), and tilting a distribution by a (trained or pre-specified) reward in reasoning tasks (Korbak et al., 2022; Geuter et al., 2025) and even protein design (Lisanza et al., 2025; Hartman et al., 2025).

In this paper, we focus on the algorithmic task of steering a pre-trained diffusion model according to a given reward function. Specifically, given a diffusion model for a base distribution p⁡(x)p(x) (which provides access to the scores of convolutions of pp with Gaussian noise), and a reward function 𝐫⁡(x)\mathbf{r}(x), our task is to sample from the tilted distribution

p⋆​(x)∝p⁡(x)​exp⁡(𝐫⁡(x)).p^{\star}(x)\propto p(x)\exp(\mathbf{r}(x)).

For any reward function 𝐫\mathbf{r}, p⋆p^{\star} has a natural variational interpretation as the solution to the KL-regularized optimization problem arg​maxq𝔼q[𝐫]−D𝖪𝖫(q∥p)\argmax_{q}\EE_{q}[\mathbf{r}]-D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(q\|p\right) (Korbak et al., 2022). Moreover, with appropriate choices of the reward function—ranging from simple quadratics to complex pre-trained reward models—the task of sampling from p⋆p^{\star} formalizes many concrete practical problems, including inpainting (Karan et al., 2025), posterior inference under noisy measurements (Bruna and Han, 2024), and human preference alignment (Singhal et al., 2025). Empirically, the algorithms used are often heuristics, and have known failure modes (Chidambaram et al., 2024). Theoretically, the algorithmic landscape for this task, and the fundamental computational barriers, remain largely unexplored—even when the reward function is very simple.

In this paper, we focus on the family of quadratic reward functions 𝐫⁡(x)=x⊤​A​x+b⊤​x\mathbf{r}(x)=x^{\top}Ax+b^{\top}x. With this family of rewards, the steering task already encapsulates several of the preceding applications (Karan et al., 2025; Bruna and Han, 2024). For example, posterior inference with linear measurements and Gaussian noise corresponds to steering with the log-density of an appropriate Gaussian: 𝐫⁡(x)=−12​σ2​‖M​x−y‖22\mathbf{r}(x)=-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\left\lVert Mx-y\right\rVert_{2}^{2}. Moreover, quadratic bonuses of the form 𝐫⁡(x)=x⊤​Σ−1​x\mathbf{r}(x)=x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}x, for positive-definite Σ\Sigma, are commonly used in applications such as rare-event sampling (Asmussen et al., 2011) and reinforcement learning (Tuyls et al., 2025), to steer towards (or optimize for) rare or novel generations.

From a theoretical perspective, steering with quadratic rewards is computationally intractable with no further assumptions (Gupta et al., 2024; Bruna and Han, 2024). Indeed, if the base distribution p⁡(x)p(x) is uniform over the discrete hypercube, then p⋆​(x)∝exp⁡(x⊤​A​x+b⊤​x)p^{\star}(x)\propto\exp(x^{\top}Ax+b^{\top}x) is precisely a classical Ising model (Ising, 1925), and a seminal line of work has shown that exact and approximate sampling from an Ising model can be intractable (Jerrum and Sinclair, 1993; Sly and Sun, 2012; Galanis et al., 2016). However, there is also a rich literature on efficient algorithms for sampling from Ising models with special structure (Jerrum and Sinclair, 1993; Eldan et al., 2022; Koehler et al., 2022; Chen and Eldan, 2022). Can these sorts of structural assumptions help explain when steering a general base measure pp accessible via a diffusion model is indeed tractable?

1.1 Contributions

In this paper, we provide a fine-grained understanding of the computational landscape of steering diffusion models with quadratic rewards 𝐫⁡(x):=x⊤​A​x+b⊤​x\mathbf{r}(x):=x^{\top}Ax+b^{\top}x. Through the lens of the rank of the quadratic form (i.e. rank⁡(A)\rank(A))—a fundamental quantity in the special case of sampling from Ising models (Koehler et al., 2022)—we delineate regimes in which the task is computationally tractable, and regimes in which it is not. Precisely, we show the following:

Linear rewards admit an efficient sampler (Section 3).

If the reward is a linear function 𝐫⁡(x)=b⊤​x\mathbf{r}(x)=b^{\top}x for some vector b∈ℝdb\in\mathbb{R}^{d} (in other words, rank⁡(A)=0\rank(A)=0), we can efficiently sample from the tilt p⋆p^{\star}. This relatively simple result was seemingly missed in prior literature, and is a consequence of the fact that the scores of p⋆p^{\star} have a simple closed-form expression in terms of the reward function and scores of the base distribution pp.

Negative-definite quadratic rewards induce intractability, even for rank-1 matrices (Section 4).

If 𝐫⁡(x)=x⊤​A​x\mathbf{r}(x)=x^{\top}Ax, where AA is a rank-11 negative semi-definite matrix, then the task of sampling from p⋆p^{\star} is computationally intractable, assuming NP⊈BPP\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{BPP}.

Positive-definite, low-rank quadratic rewards admit an efficient sampler (Section 5).

If 𝐫⁡(x)=x⊤​A​x\mathbf{r}(x)=x^{\top}Ax, where AA is a rank-O⁡(1)O(1) positive semi-definite matrix, then there is an algorithm that samples from p∗p^{*} (approximately, in Wasserstein distance) in polynomial time.11 1 We remark that the runtime also scales polynomially in ‖A‖2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{2}. This leaves a conceptual gap, since our hardness result for negative-definite rewards does not rule out an algorithm with similar scaling. We believe such an algorithm is unlikely to exist, but we defer resolution of this question to future work. For completeness, we also show that without the low-rank assumption, the problem becomes computationally intractable (Appendix A). The algorithmic result is based on the idea of using the Hubbard-Stratonovich transform (Hubbard, 1959) to construct a lifting of the target distribution (i.e. introduce a new variable). We show how to sample from this lifted distribution using sampling from linear-reward tilts as a subroutine. We believe this result is of additional conceptual interest as it shows that sampling from linear-reward tilts can be a useful building block for designing inference-time algorithms even for more complex reward models.

1.2 Related work

Several prior works have studied the problem of provably steering diffusion models with a quadratic reward function r⁡(x)=−12​σ2​‖A​x−b‖2r(x)=-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\|Ax-b\|^{2} (Gupta et al., 2024; Bruna and Han, 2024; Xun et al., 2025; Parulekar et al., 2025), motivated by the task of linear inverse problems, i.e. posterior inference with noisy linear measurements. Gupta et al. (2024) show that steering with general (i.e. potentially high-rank) negative-definite quadratic rewards is cryptographically hard, and Bruna and Han (2024) show that the same problem is intractable via reduction from the problem of sampling Ising models. Our result in Section 4 strengthens these by showing that intractability holds even when the quadratic form is rank-11.

Bruna and Han (2024) show that the hardness can be circumvented when σ\sigma is sufficiently small. In the context of inverse problems, AA corresponds to a measurement operator, and σ\sigma to a signal-to-noise ratio; the small-σ\sigma regime is easier since it makes p⋆p^{\star} more log-concave. The main tool they use is the Polchinsky flow (Bauerschmidt et al., 2024). Xun et al. (2025) develop an efficient algorithm for the same problem, without assumptions on AA and σ\sigma, but require that the base distribution pp satisfies a condition called “local log-concavity”. Parulekar et al. (2025) develop an efficient algorithm with no assumptions, but it (necessarily) has no guarantee of closeness in total variation or Wasserstein distance.

Zooming out, Chidambaram et al. (2024) analyze a popular heuristic for guidance—i.e. sampling from a class-conditioned diffusion model—and show some natural examples in which it has the intended behavior, and some examples of failure modes. Karan et al. (2025) provide a wrapper for existing heuristics, which admits a theoretical guarantee that is weaker than approximate sampling. Rohatgi et al. (2025) consider sampling from tilted distributions when pp is the law of an autoregressive language model, and reward access is augmented by a “process reward” that estimates the quality of partial generations.

Finally, at a technical level, our application of Hubbard-Stratonovich in the PSD setting is inspired by that of Koehler et al. (2022) for sampling from (approximately) low-rank Ising models, given access to their unnormalized density. Their algorithm uses the transform in conjunction with techniques from Markov Chains and variational inference, whereas ours requires building on our algorithm for linear rewards.

2 Preliminaries and notation

Notation.

For a set SS, let Δ⁡(S)\Delta(S) denote the space of distributions over SS. For R>0R>0, let ℬd,2​(R):={x∈ℝd:‖x‖2≤R}\mathscr{B}_{d,2}(R):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}\leq R\}. For a distribution pp, supp⁡(p)\supp(p) denotes its support. For distributions p,qp,q, 𝖳𝖵⁡(p,q){\mathsf{TV}}(p,q) denotes total variation distance and 𝖶2​(p,q)\mathsf{W}_{2}(p,q) denotes Wasserstein-22 distance. We let 𝒩⁡(μ,Σ)\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma) denote the Gaussian distribution with mean μ\mu and covariance Σ\Sigma.

Definition 2.1 (Noised distribution).

For any distribution q∈Δ⁡(ℝd)q\in\Delta(\mathbb{R}^{d}), for any σ∈[0,1]\sigma\in[0,1], we define qσ∈Δ⁡(ℝd)q_{\sigma}\in\Delta(\mathbb{R}^{d}) as the law of 1−σ2​X+σ​Z\sqrt{1-\sigma^{2}}X+\sigma Z where X∼qX\sim q and Z∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}).

Formal setting.

Let p∈Δ⁡(ℝd)p\in\Delta(\mathbb{R}^{d}) be a base distribution and let 𝐫⁡(x):ℝd→ℝ\mathbf{r}(x):\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be a reward function. Our goal is to (approximately) sample from the tilted distribution p⋆∈Δ⁡(ℝd)p^{\star}\in\Delta(\mathbb{R}^{d}) defined by:

p⋆​(x)∝p⁡(x)​exp⁡(𝐫⁡(x)),p^{\star}(x)\propto p(x)\exp(\mathbf{r}(x)),

which is well-defined whenever 𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(𝐫⁡(x))]<∞\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\mathbf{r}(x))]<\infty. We make the following standard boundedness assumption (De Bortoli, 2022; Chen et al., 2023), which ensures that p⋆p^{\star} is well-defined for any continuous reward; our algorithms will have runtime polynomial in the bound C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆C_{\mathsf{norm}}:

Assumption 2.2 (Boundedness).

Let C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆≥1C_{\mathsf{norm}}\geq 1. We assume that supx∈supp⁡(p)‖x‖2≤C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆\sup_{x\in\supp(p)}\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}\leq C_{\mathsf{norm}}.

We access pp via the following oracle, which is exactly the object one would have access to if a diffusion model was (pre-)trained on the distribution pp.

Assumption 2.3 (Score oracle).

For any σ∈(0,1)\sigma\in(0,1) and x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, we can query sσ​(x):=∇log⁡pσ​(x)s_{\sigma}(x):=\nabla\log p_{\sigma}(x).

Note that we assume exact access to the scores, following prior work (Bruna and Han, 2024; Parulekar et al., 2025); understanding the effect of errors is an interesting open question.

As shown by Chen et al. (2023), under Assumption 2.2, the score oracle enables efficient approximate sampling from the base distribution pp with small Wasserstein-22 error:

Theorem 2.4 (Chen et al. (2023)).

Let d,C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆∈ℕd,C_{\mathsf{norm}}\in\mathbb{N} and ϵ>0\epsilon>0. Fix q∈Δ⁡(ℝd)q\in\Delta(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Suppose that supp⁡(q)⊆ℬd,2​(C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆)\supp(q)\subseteq\mathscr{B}_{d,2}(C_{\mathsf{norm}}). There is a poly⁡(d,ϵ−1,C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆)\poly(d,\epsilon^{-1},C_{\mathsf{norm}})-time algorithm 𝖴𝗇𝖺𝖽𝗃𝗎𝗌𝗍𝖾𝖽𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾𝗋\mathsf{UnadjustedSampler} that, given parameters ϵ,C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆\epsilon,C_{\mathsf{norm}} as well as query access to ∇log⁡qσ​(x)\nabla\log q_{\sigma}(x) for any x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and σ∈(0,1)\sigma\in(0,1), produces a sample from distribution q~\widetilde{q} with 𝖶2​(q,q~)≤ϵ\mathsf{W}_{2}(q,\widetilde{q})\leq\epsilon and supp⁡(q~)⊆ℬd,2​(C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆)\supp(\widetilde{q})\subseteq\mathscr{B}_{d,2}(C_{\mathsf{norm}}).22 2 The second property is not explicitly stated by Chen et al. (2023), but it is immediate since projection onto ℬd,2​(C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆)\mathscr{B}_{d,2}(C_{\mathsf{norm}}) is contractive in ℓ2\ell_{2}.

Under stronger assumptions (e.g. Lipschitzness of the scores), the approximation in Wasserstein distance can be upgraded to approximation in total variation (Chen et al., 2023). However, in this work we focus on the minimal assumptions described above, and seek to approximately sample from p⋆p^{\star} in Wasserstein.

3 Steering with linear rewards is tractable

In this section we prove Theorem 3.2, which states that if 𝐫\mathbf{r} is a linear function, there is an efficient approximate sampler 𝖫𝗂𝗇𝖳𝗂𝗅𝗍𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾𝗋\mathsf{LinTiltSampler} (Algorithm 1) for p⋆p^{\star}. The following definition will be convenient:

Definition 3.1.

Fix v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. We define p⁡(⋅,v)∈Δ⁡(ℝd)p(\cdot;v)\in\Delta(\mathbb{R}^{d}) by p⁡(x,v)∝p⁡(x)​e⟨x,v⟩.p(x;v)\propto p(x)e^{\langle x,v\rangle}.

Theorem 3.2.

Suppose that Assumption 2.2 holds. Let v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and ϵ>0\epsilon>0. The output x~←𝖫𝗂𝗇𝖳𝗂𝗅𝗍𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾𝗋⁡((sσ)σ,v,ϵ,C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆)\widetilde{x}\leftarrow\mathsf{LinTiltSampler}((s_{\sigma})_{\sigma},v,\epsilon,C_{\mathsf{norm}}) has law p^​(⋅,v)\widehat{p}(\cdot;v) satisfying 𝖶2​(p^​(⋅,v),p⁡(⋅,v))≤ϵ\mathsf{W}_{2}(\widehat{p}(\cdot;v),p(\cdot;v))\leq\epsilon and supp⁡(p^​(⋅,v))⊆ℬd,2​(C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆)\supp(\widehat{p}(\cdot;v))\subseteq\mathscr{B}_{d,2}(C_{\mathsf{norm}}). Moreover, the time complexity of the algorithm is at most poly⁡(d,ϵ−1,C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆)\poly(d,\epsilon^{-1},C_{\mathsf{norm}}).

The key lemma facilitating this result is the following:

Lemma 3.3.

For any x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and σ≥0\sigma\geq 0, it holds that

∇log⁡pσ​(x,v)=v1−σ2+∇log⁡pσ​(x+σ21−σ2​v)\nabla\log p_{\sigma}(x;v)=\frac{v}{\sqrt{1-\sigma^{2}}}+\nabla\log p_{\sigma}\left(x+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\sqrt{1-\sigma^{2}}}v\right)
Proof.

We explicitly compute the density pσ​(x,v)p_{\sigma}(x;v). Set t:=1−σ2t:=\sqrt{1-\sigma^{2}}. Then:

pσ​(x,v)\displaystyle p_{\sigma}(x;v) =t−d(2​π​σ2)d/2∫ℝdp(t−1y;v)e−‖y−x‖22/(2σ2)dy\displaystyle=\frac{t^{-d}}{(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{d/2}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}p(t^{-1}y;v)e^{-\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert_{2}^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})}\,\mathrm{d}y
∝∫ℝdp⁡(t−1​y)​e⟨t−1​y,v⟩−‖y−x‖22/(2​σ2)​𝑑y\displaystyle\propto\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}p(t^{-1}y)e^{\langle t^{-1}y,v\rangle-\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert_{2}^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})}\,\mathrm{d}y
=e⟨t−1​x,v⟩​∫ℝdp⁡(t−1​y)​e⟨t−1​(y−x),v⟩−‖y−x‖22/(2​σ2)​𝑑y\displaystyle=e^{\langle t^{-1}x,v\rangle}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}p(t^{-1}y)e^{\langle t^{-1}(y-x),v\rangle-\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert_{2}^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})}\,\mathrm{d}y
=e⟨t−1​x,v⟩∫ℝdp(t−1y)e−‖y−x−t−1σ2v‖22/(2σ2)dy\displaystyle=e^{\langle t^{-1}x,v\rangle}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}p(t^{-1}y)e^{-\left\lVert y-x-t^{-1}\sigma^{2}v\right\rVert_{2}^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})}\,\mathrm{d}y
=e⟨t−1​x,v⟩​pσ​(x+t−1​σ2​v)\displaystyle=e^{\langle t^{-1}x,v\rangle}p_{\sigma}(x+t^{-1}\sigma^{2}v)

where the fourth equality is by completing the square. It follows that

∇log⁡pσ​(x,v)=v1−σ2+∇log⁡pσ​(x+σ21−σ2​v)\nabla\log p_{\sigma}(x;v)=\frac{v}{\sqrt{1-\sigma^{2}}}+\nabla\log p_{\sigma}\left(x+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\sqrt{1-\sigma^{2}}}v\right)

as claimed. ∎

The implication of this lemma is that using the score oracle for pp, we can efficiently simulate a score oracle for p⋆:=p⁡(⋅,v)p^{\star}:=p(\cdot;v). We can plug this result into Theorem 2.4 (due to Chen et al. (2023)), which states that for any distribution qq with bounded support, given query access to ∇log⁡qσ\nabla\log q_{\sigma} for any σ∈(0,1)\sigma\in(0,1), there is an efficient algorithm that approximately samples from qq. The proof of Theorem 3.2 is essentially immediate:

Proof of Theorem 3.2.

By Lemma 3.3, the functions sσ⋆s^{\star}_{\sigma} defined in Algorithm 1 satisfy sσ⋆​(x)=∇log⁡pσ​(x,v)s^{\star}_{\sigma}(x)=\nabla\log p_{\sigma}(x;v) for all x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and σ∈(0,1)\sigma\in(0,1). Since supp⁡(p)⊆ℬd,2​(C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆)\supp(p)\subseteq\mathscr{B}_{d,2}(C_{\mathsf{norm}}), it is immediate that supp⁡(p⁡(⋅,v))⊆ℬd,2​(C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆)\supp(p(\cdot;v))\subseteq\mathscr{B}_{d,2}(C_{\mathsf{norm}}). The claim then follows from Theorem 2.4. ■\blacksquare

4 Steering with low-rank negative-definite rewards is hard

In this section, we show that the problem of steering a diffusion model with a low-rank negative-definite reward—specifically, 𝐫⁡(x)=x⊤​A​x\mathbf{r}(x)=x^{\top}Ax, where AA is a negative semi-definite matrix of rank 11—is computationally intractable, assuming a standard conjecture (NP⊈BPP\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}) from computational complexity. This refines a result of Bruna and Han (2024) (who showed this claim for general negative semi-definite matrices AA) and combines elements of their analysis with a result of Koehler et al. (2022) (who showed that sampling from rank-11 Ising models is computationally intractable).

Theorem 4.1.

Suppose that there is a randomized algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} with the following property. For any integer d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}, any distribution p∈Δ⁡(ℝd)p\in\Delta(\mathbb{R}^{d}) satisfying Assumption 2.2 with parameter C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆≥1C_{\mathsf{norm}}\geq 1, and any rank-11, negative semi-definite A∈ℝd×dA\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, the output x~∈ℝd\widetilde{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} of 𝒜⁡((∇log⁡pσ)σ∈(0,1),A,C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆)\mathcal{A}((\nabla\log p_{\sigma})_{\sigma\in(0,1)},A,C_{\mathsf{norm}}) has law ν\nu satisfying 𝖶2​(ν,p⋆)≤1/4\mathsf{W}_{2}(\nu,p^{\star})\leq 1/4, where p⋆∈Δ⁡(ℝd)p^{\star}\in\Delta(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is the tilted distribution

p⋆​(x)∝p⁡(x)​exp⁡(x⊤​A​x).p^{\star}(x)\propto p(x)\exp(x^{\top}Ax).

Moreover, the time complexity of 𝒜⁡((∇log⁡pσ)σ∈(0,1),w,C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆)\mathcal{A}((\nabla\log p_{\sigma})_{\sigma\in(0,1)},w,C_{\mathsf{norm}}) is poly⁡(d,C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆)\poly(d,C_{\mathsf{norm}}).

Then, NP⊆BPP\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}.

As a caveat, Theorem 4.1 does not rule out an algorithm with time complexity that also scales polynomially in ‖A‖2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{2}. We will prove Theorem 4.1 by reducing from the NP\mathrm{NP}-hard PARTITION problem (Karp, 1975), defined as follows:

Definition 4.2 (PARTITION).

Given integers w:=(a1,…,ad)∈ℤdw:=(a_{1},\dots,a_{d})\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}, the PARTITION problem is to decide whether there exists x∈{±1}dx\in\{\pm 1\}^{d} such that w⊤​x=0.w^{\top}x=0.

Given an instance w∈ℤdw\in\mathbb{Z}^{d} of the partition problem, we will define a base distribution p∈Δ⁡(ℝd)p\in\Delta(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and matrix Aw∈ℝd×dA_{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} as follows:

p:=Unif⁡({−1,1}d)=2−d​∑x∈{±1}dδx∈Δ⁡(ℝd),Aw:=−(d+5)​w​w⊤⪯0.p:=\Unif(\{-1,1\}^{d})=2^{-d}\sum_{x\in\{\pm 1\}^{d}}\delta_{x}\in\Delta(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\qquad A_{w}:=-(d+5)\,ww^{\top}\preceq 0.

For notational convenience, we then define qw∈Δ⁡(ℝd)q_{w}\in\Delta(\mathbb{R}^{d}) to be the tilted distribution

qw​(x)∝p⁡(x)​exp⁡(x⊤​Aw​x).q_{w}(x)\propto p(x)\exp(x^{\top}A_{w}x).

Note that since pσp_{\sigma} is a product distribution for each σ∈(0,1)\sigma\in(0,1), and each marginal is a mixture of two Gaussians, the score oracle for pp can be simulated efficiently. Moreover, intuitively, the tilted distribution qwq_{w} will be concentrated on x∈{−1,1}dx\in\{-1,1\}^{d} with ⟨x,w⟩≈0\langle x,w\rangle\approx 0. Thus, if ν\nu is close to qwq_{w} in Wasserstein distance, then ν\nu will be concentrated near such xx.

The following lemma helps formalize this intuition by lower bounding the mass of the tilted distribution on solutions to the PARTITION problem, in the event that the tilt corresponds to a YES instance of the PARTITION problem. We show:

Lemma 4.3.

Given a PARTITION instance w∈ℤdw\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}, define the set Sw:={x∈{±1}d:w⊤​x=0}S_{w}:=\{x\in\{\pm 1\}^{d}:w^{\top}x=0\}. Assume Sw≠∅S_{w}\neq\emptyset (i.e. the PARTITION instance is a YES instance). Then qw​(Sw)≥200201.q_{w}(S_{w})\;\geq\;\frac{200}{201}.

See Section B.1 for the proof. With this lemma in hand, we can prove Theorem 4.1:

Proof of Theorem 4.1.

Given a PARTITION instance w∈ℤnw\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}, construct pp and AwA_{w} as above, and consider the corresponding tilted distribution p⋆=qwp^{\star}=q_{w} supported on {±1}d\{\pm 1\}^{d}. Set C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆:=dC_{\mathsf{norm}}:=\sqrt{d} and note that Assumption 2.2 is satisfied. Define the set Sw:={x∈{±1}n:w⊤​x=0}S_{w}:=\{x\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}:w^{\top}x=0\} and define

RSw:={y∈ℝn:sgn⁡(y)∈Sw}.R_{S_{w}}:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:{\rm sgn}(y)\in S_{w}\}.

For σ∈(0,1)\sigma\in(0,1), let sσ:=∇log⁡pσs_{\sigma}:=\nabla\log p_{\sigma}, and note that we can efficiently simulate queries to sσs_{\sigma} for any x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. To solve the PARTITION problem, we will run the sampler 𝒜⁡((sσ)σ∈(0,1),Aw,C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆)\mathcal{A}((s_{\sigma})_{\sigma\in(0,1)},A_{w},C_{\mathsf{norm}}) to obtain Y∈ℝnY\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. We will then round the output to compute x^:=sgn⁡(Y)∈{±1}n\widehat{x}:={\rm sgn}(Y)\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}. We will output YES iff w⊤​x^=0w^{\top}\widehat{x}=0.

We analyze what happens in the YES and NO cases.

If the PARTITION instance is NO, then Sw=∅S_{w}=\emptyset. In that case, for every x^∈{±1}n\widehat{x}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}, we have w⊤​x^≠0w^{\top}\widehat{x}\neq 0, so the above algorithm always outputs NO.

In the YES case, we have Sw≠∅S_{w}\neq\emptyset. Let νw\nu_{w} be the output distribution of YY. By assumption, 𝖶2​(νw,qw)≤1/4\mathsf{W}_{2}(\nu_{w},q_{w})\leq 1/4. Applying Lemma B.1 with μ:=qw\mu:=q_{w}, ν:=νw\nu:=\nu_{w}, and S:=SwS:=S_{w}, we obtain

νw​(RSw)≥qw​(Sw)−(1/4)2.\nu_{w}(R_{S_{w}})\;\geq\;q_{w}(S_{w})-(1/4)^{2}.

By Lemma 4.3, qw​(Sw)≥200201q_{w}(S_{w})\geq\frac{200}{201}. Plugging in these numbers, we get νw​(RSw)>0.9.\nu_{w}(R_{S_{w}})>0.9. Thus, this algorithm decides PARTITION with one-sided error: it always outputs NO on NO instances, and outputs YES on YES instances with probability at least 0.90.9. Moreover, by assumption on 𝒜\mathcal{A}, the time complexity of this algorithm is poly⁡(d)\poly(d). It follows that NP⊆BPP\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}. ■\blacksquare

5 Steering with low-rank positive-definite rewards is tractable

In this section, we show that the problem of steering a diffusion model with low-rank positive-definite rewards, i.e. with 𝐫⁡(x)=x⊤​A​x\mathbf{r}(x)=x^{\top}Ax for positive semi-definite low-rank AA, is computationally tractable. Without loss of generality, we may write A=12​L⊤​LA=\frac{1}{2}L^{\top}L where LL is an r×dr\times d matrix. Then the tilted distribution p⋆p^{\star} is as defined below:

Definition 5.1.

Fix p∈Δ⁡(ℝd)p\in\Delta(\mathbb{R}^{d}) satisfying Assumption 2.2 with parameter C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆C_{\mathsf{norm}}. Fix a matrix L∈ℝr×dL\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d}. We define p⋆∈Δ⁡(ℝd)p^{\star}\in\Delta(\mathbb{R}^{d}) by

p⋆​(x):=p⁡(x)​e12​‖L​x‖22Zp^{\star}(x):=\frac{p(x)e^{\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert Lx\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}}{Z}

where Z:=𝔼x∼p[e12​‖Lx‖22]Z:=\EE_{x\sim p}[e^{\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert Lx\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}] is the normalization constant.

Note that ZZ is finite by Assumption 2.2, and hence p⋆p^{\star} is well-defined. The main result of this section is the following theorem, which shows that 𝖯𝖲𝖣𝖳𝗂𝗅𝗍𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾𝗋\mathsf{PSDTiltSampler} (Algorithm 2) samples from p⋆p^{\star} in polynomial time whenever r=O⁡(1)r=O(1) (and C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆C_{\mathsf{norm}} and ‖L‖2\left\lVert L\right\rVert_{2} are polynomially bounded):

Theorem 5.2.

Suppose that Assumption 2.2 holds. Let D≥1D\geq 1 and ϵ𝖿𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗅∈(0,1/2)\epsilon_{\mathsf{final}}\in(0,1/2). Suppose that D≥supx∈supp⁡(p)‖L​x‖2D\geq\sup_{x\in\supp(p)}\left\lVert Lx\right\rVert_{2}. Then the output x~\widetilde{x} of 𝖯𝖲𝖣𝖳𝗂𝗅𝗍𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾𝗋⁡((sσ)σ,L,D,C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆,ϵ𝖿𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗅)\mathsf{PSDTiltSampler}((s_{\sigma})_{\sigma},L,D,C_{\mathsf{norm}},\epsilon_{\mathsf{final}}) has law μ\mu satisfying 𝖶2​(μ,p⋆)≤ϵ𝖿𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗅\mathsf{W}_{2}(\mu,p^{\star})\leq\epsilon_{\mathsf{final}}. Moreover, the time complexity of the algorithm is at most

poly⁡(d,C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆,‖L‖2,Dr,rr,ϵ𝖿𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗅−r).\poly(d,C_{\mathsf{norm}},\left\lVert L\right\rVert_{2},D^{r},r^{r},\epsilon_{\mathsf{final}}^{-r}).

The key insight is the following decomposition, leveraging the Hubbard-Stratonovich (Hubbard, 1959) transform:

Definition 5.3.

For each z∈ℝrz\in\mathbb{R}^{r}, define Z⁡(z):=∫ℝdp⁡(x)​e⟨L​x,z⟩​𝑑xZ(z):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}p(x)e^{\langle Lx,z\rangle}\,\mathrm{d}x.

As before, Z⁡(z)Z(z) is finite by Assumption 2.2.

Lemma 5.4.

It holds for all x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} that

p⋆​(x)=(2π)−d/2Z​∫ℝrZ⁡(z)​e−12​‖z‖22​p​(x,L⊤​z)​𝑑z.p^{\star}(x)=\frac{(2\pi)^{-d/2}}{Z}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{r}}Z(z)e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert z\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}p(x;L^{\top}z)\,\mathrm{d}z.
Proof.

The Hubbard-Stratonovich transform gives

e12​‖L​x‖22=(2π)−d/2∫ze−12​‖z‖22+⟨L​x,z⟩dz.e^{\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert Lx\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\int_{z}e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert z\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\langle Lx,z\rangle}\,\mathrm{d}z.

It follows that

p⋆​(x)\displaystyle p^{\star}(x) =(2π)−d/2∫ℝre−12​‖z‖22+⟨L​x,z⟩p(x)dzZ\displaystyle=\frac{(2\pi)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{r}}e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert z\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\langle Lx,z\rangle}p(x)\,\mathrm{d}z}{Z}
=(2π)−d/2∫ℝrZ(z)e−12​‖z‖22p(x;L⊤z)dzZ\displaystyle=\frac{(2\pi)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{r}}Z(z)e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert z\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}p(x;L^{\top}z)\,\mathrm{d}z}{Z}

as claimed. ∎

The above decomposition implies that p⋆p^{\star} is the marginal distribution of xx under the following lifted distribution in ℝd+r\mathbb{R}^{d+r}:

q⁡(x,z)∝Z⁡(z)​e−12​‖z‖22​p​(x,L⊤​z).q(x,z)\propto Z(z)e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert z\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}p(x;L^{\top}z).

For any fixed zz, the conditional distribution q⁡(x∣z)q(x\mid{}z) is precisely p⁡(x,L⊤​z)p(x;L^{\top}z), which we can efficiently sample from using Algorithm 1 from Section 3. Thus, it suffices to (approximately) sample from the marginal distribution over zz, which is precisely q⁡(z)∝Z⁡(z)​e−12​‖z‖22q(z)\propto Z(z)e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert z\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}. This is where we exploit the low-rank assumption: since zz is rr-dimensional, and p⁡(x,L⊤​z)p(x;L^{\top}z) satisfies appropriate smoothness in zz, it suffices to explicitly estimate the densities q⁡(z)q(z) for zz on a grid of cardinality (roughly) exp⁡(r)\exp(r). We accomplish this using 𝖤𝗌𝗍𝗂𝗆𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖭𝗈𝗋𝗆𝖺𝗅𝗂𝗓𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇\mathsf{EstimateNormalization} (Algorithm 3), which approximates Z⁡(z)Z(z) (given the vector v=L⊤​zv=L^{\top}z) by telescoping Monte Carlo approximations. See Algorithm 2 for the pseudocode.

Remark 5.5.

A natural alternative approach to sample from q⁡(x,z)q(x,z) would be Gibbs sampling: i.e. alternately sample from q⁡(x∣z)q(x\mid{}z) and q⁡(z∣x)q(z\mid{}x), using that both conditional distributions are tractable. However, examples can be constructed in which the Markov chains does not mix rapidly. In particular, if pp is a mixture of two Gaussians defined as p=12​𝒩​(−u,σ2​I)+12​𝒩​(u,σ2​I)p=\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{N}(-u,\sigma^{2}I)+\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{N}(u,\sigma^{2}I), and we tilt with a quadratic reward 𝐫⁡(x)=λ​u​u⊤\mathbf{r}(x)=\lambda uu^{\top}, it can be seen that q⁡(z|x)=𝒩⁡(2​λ​u⊤​x,1)​(z)q(z|x)=\mathcal{N}(\sqrt{2\lambda}u^{\top}x,1)(z) and q⁡(x|z)∝p⁡(x)​exp⁡(2​λ​z​u⊤​x)q(x|z)\propto p(x)\exp(\sqrt{2\lambda}zu^{\top}x). So, if zz is positive, then q⁡(x|z)q(x|z) is biased towards the +u+u mode, and q⁡(z|x)q(z|x) has positive mean ≈2​λ​‖u‖2\approx\sqrt{2\lambda}\|u\|^{2} so it will remain positive. Thus, the tilt induces a metastability of the Gibbs sampler.

In Section 5.1, we analyze the subroutine 𝖤𝗌𝗍𝗂𝗆𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖭𝗈𝗋𝗆𝖺𝗅𝗂𝗓𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇\mathsf{EstimateNormalization}. In Section 5.2 we complete the proof of Theorem 5.2.

5.1 Analysis of 𝖤𝗌𝗍𝗂𝗆𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖭𝗈𝗋𝗆𝖺𝗅𝗂𝗓𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇\mathsf{EstimateNormalization}

Given z∈ℝrz\in\mathbb{R}^{r}, a first attempt at estimating Z⁡(z)Z(z) would be Monte Carlo estimation using samples from pp. However, this could take exponential time in the problem parameters. Instead, we observe that for any sufficiently close z,z′∈ℝrz,z^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{r}, it is possible to efficiently estimate Z⁡(z)/Z⁡(z′)Z(z)/Z(z^{\prime}) using samples from p⁡(⋅,L⊤​z′)p(\cdot;L^{\top}z^{\prime})—which we can (approximately) obtain using 𝖫𝗂𝗇𝖳𝗂𝗅𝗍𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾𝗋\mathsf{LinTiltSampler}. Thus, we can estimate Z⁡(z)Z(z) by telescoping along a path from Z⁡(0)=1Z(0)=1. This idea is formalized in Algorithm 3 and analyzed in Lemma 5.6 below.

Lemma 5.6.

Let v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, ϵ,δ∈(0,1/2)\epsilon,\delta\in(0,1/2), and N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}. Suppose that N≥C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆​‖v‖2N\geq C_{\mathsf{norm}}\left\lVert v\right\rVert_{2}. Then the output κ^←𝖤𝗌𝗍𝗂𝗆𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖭𝗈𝗋𝗆𝖺𝗅𝗂𝗓𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇⁡((sσ)σ,v,ϵ,δ,C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆)\hat{\kappa}\leftarrow\mathsf{EstimateNormalization}((s_{\sigma})_{\sigma},v,\epsilon,\delta,C_{\mathsf{norm}}) satisfies

κ^𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(⟨x,v⟩)]∈[1−ϵ,1+ϵ]\frac{\hat{\kappa}}{\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\langle x,v\rangle)]}\in[1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon] (1)

with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. Moreover, the time complexity of the algorithm is at most

poly⁡(d,ϵ−1,C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆,‖v‖2,log⁡(1/δ)).\poly(d,\epsilon^{-1},C_{\mathsf{norm}},\left\lVert v\right\rVert_{2},\log(1/\delta)).
Proof.

Fix 1≤n≤N1\leq n\leq N. Set u:=(n−1)N​vu:=\frac{(n-1)}{N}v and w:=nN​vw:=\frac{n}{N}v. Let p^​(⋅,u)\widehat{p}(\cdot;u) denote the law of

𝖫𝗂𝗇𝖳𝗂𝗅𝗍𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾𝗋⁡((sσ)σ,u,ϵ′,C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆).\mathsf{LinTiltSampler}((s_{\sigma})_{\sigma},u,\epsilon^{\prime},C_{\mathsf{norm}}).

By Theorem 3.2, we have 𝖶2​(p^​(⋅,u),p⁡(⋅,u))≤ϵ′\mathsf{W}_{2}(\widehat{p}(\cdot;u),p(\cdot;u))\leq\epsilon^{\prime} and supp⁡(p^​(⋅,u))⊆ℬd,2​(C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆)\supp(\widehat{p}(\cdot;u))\subseteq\mathscr{B}_{d,2}(C_{\mathsf{norm}}).

Define ξ(m):=exp⁡(⟨x(m),1N​v⟩)\xi^{\footnotesize(m)}:=\exp(\langle x^{\footnotesize(m)},\frac{1}{N}v\rangle) for 1≤m≤M1\leq m\leq M. Observe that ξ(1),…,ξ(M)\xi^{\footnotesize(1)},\dots,\xi^{\footnotesize(M)} are i.i.d. random variables with ξ(m)∈[0,e]\xi^{\footnotesize(m)}\in[0,e] almost surely (by assumption on NN, and the fact that p^​(⋅,u)\widehat{p}(\cdot;u) is supported on ℬd,2​(C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆)\mathscr{B}_{d,2}(C_{\mathsf{norm}})), and 𝔼[ξ(m)]=𝔼x∼p^​(⋅,u)[exp⁡(⟨x,1N​v⟩)]\EE[\xi^{\footnotesize(m)}]=\EE_{x\sim\widehat{p}(\cdot;u)}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{1}{N}v\rangle)]. It follows from Hoeffding’s inequality and choice of MM that with probability at least 1−δ/N1-\delta/N,

|κ^​(n)−𝔼x∼p^​(⋅,u)[exp⁡(⟨x,1N​v⟩)]|≤ϵ′.\left|\hat{\kappa}(n)-\EE_{x\sim\widehat{p}(\cdot;u)}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{1}{N}v\rangle)]\right|\leq\epsilon^{\prime}.

Moreover, since x↦exx\mapsto e^{x} is ee-Lipschitz in (−∞,1](-\infty,1], we can bound

|𝔼x∼p^​(⋅,u)[exp⁡(⟨x,1N​v⟩)]−𝔼x∼p⁡(⋅,u)[exp⁡(⟨x,1N​v⟩)]|\displaystyle\left|\EE_{x\sim\widehat{p}(\cdot;u)}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{1}{N}v\rangle)]-\EE_{x\sim p(\cdot;u)}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{1}{N}v\rangle)]\right| ≤e​𝖶2​(p^​(⋅,u),p⁡(⋅,u))​‖v‖2N\displaystyle\leq\frac{e\mathsf{W}_{2}(\widehat{p}(\cdot;u),p(\cdot;u))\left\lVert v\right\rVert_{2}}{N}
≤e​ϵ′.\displaystyle\leq e\epsilon^{\prime}.

|κ^​(n)−𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(⟨x,nN​v⟩)]𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(⟨x,n−1N​v⟩)]|\displaystyle\left|\hat{\kappa}(n)-\frac{\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{n}{N}v\rangle)]}{\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{n-1}{N}v\rangle)]}\right| =|κ^​(n)−𝔼x∼p⁡(⋅,u)[exp⁡(⟨x,1N​v⟩)]|\displaystyle=\left|\hat{\kappa}(n)-\EE_{x\sim p(\cdot;u)}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{1}{N}v\rangle)]\right|
≤(1+e)​ϵ′.\displaystyle\leq(1+e)\epsilon^{\prime}.

𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(⟨x,nN​v⟩)]𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(⟨x,n−1N​v⟩)]=𝔼x∼p⁡(⋅,u)[exp⁡(⟨x,1N​v⟩)]≥1/e,\frac{\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{n}{N}v\rangle)]}{\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{n-1}{N}v\rangle)]}=\EE_{x\sim p(\cdot;u)}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{1}{N}v\rangle)]\geq 1/e,

in the above event we have

|κ^​(n)⋅𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(⟨x,n−1N​v⟩)]𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(⟨x,nN​v⟩)]−1|≤(1+e)​ϵ′⋅𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(⟨x,n−1N​v⟩)]𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(⟨x,nN​v⟩)]≤(1+e)​e​ϵ′.\left|\frac{\hat{\kappa}(n)\cdot\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{n-1}{N}v\rangle)]}{\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{n}{N}v\rangle)]}-1\right|\leq(1+e)\epsilon^{\prime}\cdot\frac{\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{n-1}{N}v\rangle)]}{\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{n}{N}v\rangle)]}\leq(1+e)e\epsilon^{\prime}.

By the union bound, we have with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta that

κ^\displaystyle\hat{\kappa} =∏n=1Nκ^​(n)\displaystyle=\prod_{n=1}^{N}\hat{\kappa}(n)
≤∏n=1N(1+(1+e)​e​ϵ′)​𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(⟨x,nN​v⟩)]𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(⟨x,n−1N​v⟩)]\displaystyle\leq\prod_{n=1}^{N}(1+(1+e)e\epsilon^{\prime})\frac{\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{n}{N}v\rangle)]}{\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{n-1}{N}v\rangle)]}
≤exp⁡((1+e)​e​ϵ′​N)​∏n=1N𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(⟨x,nN​v⟩)]𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(⟨x,n−1N​v⟩)]\displaystyle\leq\exp((1+e)e\epsilon^{\prime}N)\prod_{n=1}^{N}\frac{\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{n}{N}v\rangle)]}{\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{n-1}{N}v\rangle)]}
≤(1+ϵ)​𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(⟨x,v⟩)]\displaystyle\leq(1+\epsilon)\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\langle x,v\rangle)]

so long as ϵ′≤ϵ2​(1+e)​e​N\epsilon^{\prime}\leq\frac{\epsilon}{2(1+e)eN}, and similarly

κ^\displaystyle\hat{\kappa} ≥∏n=1N(1−(1+e)​e​ϵ′)​𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(⟨x,nN​v⟩)]𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(⟨x,n−1N​v⟩)]\displaystyle\geq\prod_{n=1}^{N}(1-(1+e)e\epsilon^{\prime})\frac{\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{n}{N}v\rangle)]}{\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{n-1}{N}v\rangle)]}
≥exp⁡(−2​(1+e)​e​ϵ′​N)​∏n=1N𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(⟨x,nN​v⟩)]𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(⟨x,n−1N​v⟩)]\displaystyle\geq\exp(-2(1+e)e\epsilon^{\prime}N)\prod_{n=1}^{N}\frac{\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{n}{N}v\rangle)]}{\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\langle x,\frac{n-1}{N}v\rangle)]}
≥(1−ϵ)​𝔼x∼p[exp⁡(⟨x,v⟩)],\displaystyle\geq(1-\epsilon)\EE_{x\sim p}[\exp(\langle x,v\rangle)],

which completes the proof of Eq. 1. The time complexity of 𝖤𝗌𝗍𝗂𝗆𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖭𝗈𝗋𝗆𝖺𝗅𝗂𝗓𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇\mathsf{EstimateNormalization} is dominated by M​NMN calls to 𝖫𝗂𝗇𝖳𝗂𝗅𝗍𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾𝗋\mathsf{LinTiltSampler}. Thus, the claimed time complexity bound follows from Theorem 3.2 and choice of N,MN,M. ∎

5.2 Analysis of 𝖯𝖲𝖣𝖳𝗂𝗅𝗍𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾𝗋\mathsf{PSDTiltSampler}

There are three types of errors in 𝖯𝖲𝖣𝖳𝗂𝗅𝗍𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾𝗋\mathsf{PSDTiltSampler} to handle: (1) error from estimation of the normalization constants Z⁡(z)Z(z), which is bounded using Lemma 5.6; (2) error in sampling from p⁡(⋅,z~)p(\cdot;\widetilde{z}), which is bounded using Theorem 3.2, and (3) error due to discretization of the Hubbard-Stratonovich transform, for which the bound is deferred to Lemma C.1. 6 Conclusion

In this paper, we considered the task of sampling from a diffusion model, tilted by a quadratic reward. We provide a fine-grained analysis of the computational tractability of this task through the lens of the rank of the quadratic form. In particular, this task is computationally intractable even for rank-1 negative-definite tilts. For low-rank positive-definite tilts, we give an efficient algorithm based on two conceptually new algorithmic ingredients: sampling from linearly tilted diffusion models, and the Hubbard-Stratonovich transform.

There are many natural directions for further work. Our results, like many other results in the literature, assume that the score oracle is exact—whereas in practice, the oracle we have access to is trained, and thus would have errors. Handling errors is non-trivial because they will be small on average under the base distribution—but algorithms which sample from the tilted distribution may deviate substantially from the trajectories that would arise when sampling from the base distribution.

Towards handling more complex rewards, it would also be interesting to understand what interaction between the structure of the reward and the structure of the base distribution allow for efficient algorithms.

Appendix A Steering with general positive-definite rewards is hard

In this section we prove the following hardness result, which shows that the low-rank assumption in Theorem 5.2 cannot be removed.

Theorem A.1.

Suppose that there is a randomized algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} with the following property. For any integer d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}, any distribution p∈Δ⁡(ℝd)p\in\Delta(\mathbb{R}^{d}) satisfying Assumption 2.2 with parameter C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆≥1C_{\mathsf{norm}}\geq 1, and any positive semi-definite A∈ℝd×dA\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, the output x~∈ℝd\widetilde{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} of 𝒜⁡((∇log⁡pσ)σ∈(0,1),A,C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆)\mathcal{A}((\nabla\log p_{\sigma})_{\sigma\in(0,1)},A,C_{\mathsf{norm}}) has law ν\nu satisfying 𝖶2​(ν,p⋆)≤1/4\mathsf{W}_{2}(\nu,p^{\star})\leq 1/4, where p⋆∈Δ⁡(ℝd)p^{\star}\in\Delta(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is the tilted distribution

p⋆​(x)∝p⁡(x)​exp⁡(x⊤​A​x).p^{\star}(x)\propto p(x)\exp(x^{\top}Ax).

Moreover, the time complexity of 𝒜⁡((∇log⁡pσ)σ∈(0,1),w,C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆)\mathcal{A}((\nabla\log p_{\sigma})_{\sigma\in(0,1)},w,C_{\mathsf{norm}}) is poly⁡(d,C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆,‖A‖2)\poly(d,C_{\mathsf{norm}},\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{2}).

Then, NP⊆BPP\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}.

We prove Theorem A.1 by reduction from the NP\mathrm{NP}-hard problem MAX-CUT:

Definition A.2 (MAX-CUT).

Given a graph G=([d],E)G=([d],E) and an integer kk, the MAX-CUT problem is to determine whether there is a set S⊆[d]S\subseteq[d] such that cG​(S)≥kc_{G}(S)\geq k, where

cG​(S):=|{(u,v)∈E:(u∈S​ and ​v∉S)​ or ​(u∉S​ and ​v∈S)}|.c_{G}(S):=|\{(u,v)\in E:(u\in S\text{ and }v\not\in S)\text{ or }(u\not\in S\text{ and }v\in S)\}|.

The proof is analogous to that of Theorem 4.1: given an instance of MAX-CUT, we construct a tilting problem so that p⋆p^{\star} puts most of its mass on solutions to the instance.

Proof of Theorem A.1.

We give an algorithm for MAX-CUT using 𝒜\mathcal{A} as a subroutine. Fix an instance of MAX-CUT, which is described by a graph G=([d],E)G=([d],E) and integer kk. Define p:=Unif⁡({0,1}d)p:=\Unif(\{0,1\}^{d}) and β:=d+100\beta:=d+100 and C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆=dC_{\mathsf{norm}}=\sqrt{d} and

A:=β⁡(∑(u,v)∈E(eu​u+ev​v−eu​v−ev​u))∈ℝd×dA:=\beta\left(\sum_{(u,v)\in E}(e_{uu}+e_{vv}-e_{uv}-e_{vu})\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}

where ei​je_{ij} is the d×dd\times d matrix with a 11 in entry (i,j)(i,j) and 00 everywhere else. We sample x~∈ℝd\widetilde{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} from 𝒜⁡((sσ)σ∈(0,1),A,C𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆)\mathcal{A}((s_{\sigma})_{\sigma\in(0,1)},A,C_{\mathsf{norm}}), where sσ=∇log⁡pσs_{\sigma}=\nabla\log p_{\sigma}, using the fact that pσp_{\sigma} is a product distribution where each marginal is a mixture of two Gaussians, and hence the score ∇log⁡pσ​(x)\nabla\log p_{\sigma}(x) can be explicitly evaluated for any xx. We then compute x^∈{0,1}d\hat{x}\in\{0,1\}^{d} defined by x^i:=𝟙[x~i≥1/2]\hat{x}_{i}:=\mathbbm{1}[\widetilde{x}_{i}\geq 1/2] for each i∈[d]i\in[d]. We return YES if β−1​x^⊤​A​x^≥k\beta^{-1}\hat{x}^{\top}A\hat{x}\geq k and NO otherwise.

Analysis.

Observe that for any x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

β−1​x⊤​A​x=∑(u,v)∈E(xu2+xv2−2​xu​xv)=∑(u,v)∈E(xu−xv)2≥0\beta^{-1}x^{\top}Ax=\sum_{(u,v)\in E}(x_{u}^{2}+x_{v}^{2}-2x_{u}x_{v})=\sum_{(u,v)\in E}(x_{u}-x_{v})^{2}\geq 0

and thus AA is positive semi-definite. Moreover, if x=𝟙​[S]x=\mathbbm{1}[S] for some S⊂[d]S\subset[d], then we have

β−1​x⊤​A​x=cG​(S).\beta^{-1}x^{\top}Ax=c_{G}(S).

p⋆​(x)∝p⁡(x)​exp⁡(x⊤​A​x).p^{\star}(x)\propto p(x)\exp(x^{\top}Ax).

Let U⊂{−1,1}dU\subset\{-1,1\}^{d} be the set of xx such that β−1​x⊤​A​x=maxy∈{−1,1}d⁡β−1​y⊤​A​y=:cG\beta^{-1}x^{\top}Ax=\max_{y\in\{-1,1\}^{d}}\beta^{-1}y^{\top}Ay=:c_{G}. Then

≤2d​exp⁡(β⁡(cG−1))exp⁡(β​cG)+2d​exp⁡(β⁡(cG−1))\displaystyle\leq\frac{2^{d}\exp(\beta(c_{G}-1))}{\exp(\beta c_{G})+2^{d}\exp(\beta(c_{G}-1))}

by choice of β\beta. Let ν\nu be the law of the sample x~\widetilde{x}. By assumption, we have 𝖶2​(ν,p⋆)≤1/4\mathsf{W}_{2}(\nu,p^{\star})\leq 1/4. Let V:={y∈ℝd:𝟙[y≥1/2]∈U}V:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\mathbbm{1}[y\geq 1/2]\in U\} where 𝟙[y≥1/2]\mathbbm{1}[y\geq 1/2] refers to the coordinate-wise thresholding of yy. Thus, the rounded vector x^\hat{x} satisfies β−1​x^⊤​A​x^=cG\beta^{-1}\hat{x}^{\top}A\hat{x}=c_{G} with probability at least 0.90.9. If the answer to the MAX-CUT instance is NO, then the output is always NO, since it holds almost surely that β−1​x^⊤​A​x^=cG​(S)≤cG<k\beta^{-1}\hat{x}^{\top}A\hat{x}=c_{G}(S)\leq c_{G}<k where x^=𝟙​[S]\hat{x}=\mathbbm{1}[S]. Moreover, the time complexity of the reduction is poly⁡(d)\poly(d) by assumption. Thus, NP⊆BPP\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}. ■\blacksquare

Appendix B Omitted details from Section 4

The following lemma lower bounds the Wasserstein distance between a distribution on the hypercube μ\mu and any other distribution ν\nu in terms of the measure that ν\nu puts on the “rounding” of the measure onto the hypercube:

Lemma B.1.

Let μ\mu be any probability measure supported on {±1}d\{\pm 1\}^{d}, let S⊆{±1}dS\subseteq\{\pm 1\}^{d}, and let ν\nu be any probability measure on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with finite second moment. Let RS:={y∈ℝd:sgn⁡(y)∈S}.R_{S}:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:{\rm sgn}(y)\in S\}. Then:

W2​(μ,ν)2≥μ⁡(S)−ν⁡(RS).W_{2}(\mu,\nu)^{2}\;\geq\;\mu(S)-\nu(R_{S}).

Thus, if W2​(μ,ν)≤εW_{2}(\mu,\nu)\leq\varepsilon, then

ν⁡(RS)≥μ⁡(S)−ε2.\nu(R_{S})\;\geq\;\mu(S)-\varepsilon^{2}.
Proof.

Fix an arbitrary coupling (X,Y)(X,Y) of μ\mu and ν\nu, i.e. X∼μX\sim\mu and Y∼νY\sim\nu. Define the event

E:={X∈SandY∉RS}.E:=\{X\in S\ \text{and}\ Y\notin R_{S}\}.

On EE, we have X∈S⊆{±1}nX\in S\subseteq\{\pm 1\}^{n}, while Y∉RSY\notin R_{S} means sgn⁡(Y)∉S{\rm sgn}(Y)\notin S. In particular, since X∈SX\in S but sgn⁡(Y)∉S{\rm sgn}(Y)\notin S, we must have sgn⁡(Y)≠X{\rm sgn}(Y)\neq X. Therefore, on the event EE we have ‖X−Y‖22≥1\|X-Y\|_{2}^{2}\geq 1. Consequently,

𝔼​‖X−Y‖22≥𝔼⁡[‖X−Y‖22⋅𝟏E]≥𝔼⁡[𝟏E]=ℙ⁡(E).\mathbb{E}\|X-Y\|_{2}^{2}\;\geq\;\mathbb{E}\big[\|X-Y\|_{2}^{2}\cdot\mathbf{1}_{E}\big]\;\geq\;\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_{E}]\;=\;\mathbb{P}(E).

Next we lower bound ℙ⁡(E)\mathbb{P}(E). Since ℙ⁡(E)=ℙ⁡(X∈S)−ℙ⁡(X∈S,Y∈RS)\mathbb{P}(E)=\mathbb{P}(X\in S)-\mathbb{P}(X\in S,\ Y\in R_{S}), and since ℙ⁡(X∈S)=μ⁡(S)\mathbb{P}(X\in S)=\mu(S) and ℙ⁡(X∈S,Y∈RS)≤ℙ⁡(Y∈RS)=ν⁡(RS)\mathbb{P}(X\in S,\ Y\in R_{S})\leq\mathbb{P}(Y\in R_{S})=\nu(R_{S}), we get:

ℙ⁡(E)≥μ⁡(S)−ν⁡(RS).\mathbb{P}(E)\;\geq\;\mu(S)-\nu(R_{S}).

Combining the two inequalities, we get that for an arbitrary coupling (X,Y)(X,Y),

𝔼​‖X−Y‖22≥μ⁡(S)−ν⁡(RS).\mathbb{E}\|X-Y\|_{2}^{2}\;\geq\;\mu(S)-\nu(R_{S}).

Taking the infimum over all couplings gives

W2​(μ,ν)2=inf𝔼​‖X−Y‖22≥μ⁡(S)−ν⁡(RS),W_{2}(\mu,\nu)^{2}=\inf\mathbb{E}\|X-Y\|_{2}^{2}\;\geq\;\mu(S)-\nu(R_{S}),

which is what we wanted. ∎

Lemma B.2 (Restatement of Lemma 4.3).

Given a PARTITION instance w∈ℤdw\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}, define the set Sw:={x∈{±1}d:w⊤​x=0}S_{w}:=\{x\in\{\pm 1\}^{d}:w^{\top}x=0\}. Assume Sw≠∅S_{w}\neq\emptyset (i.e. the PARTITION instance is a YES instance). Then qw​(Sw)≥200201q_{w}(S_{w})\;\geq\;\frac{200}{201}, where qw∈Δ⁡(ℝd)q_{w}\in\Delta(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is defined by qw​(x)∝exp⁡(−(d+5)​⟨x,w⟩2)q_{w}(x)\propto\exp(-(d+5)\langle x,w\rangle^{2}).

Proof.

qw​(x)=exp⁡(−β​(w⊤​x)2)Z~w.q_{w}(x)\;=\;\frac{\exp\!\big(-\beta(w^{\top}x)^{2}\big)}{\widetilde{Z}_{w}}.

Therefore

≤8​ϵ⋅∑z∈S∫B⁡(z)∫ℝdZ⁡(z′)​e−12​‖z′‖22​p​(x,z′)​𝑑x​d​z′\displaystyle\leq 8\epsilon\cdot\sum_{z\in S}\int_{B(z)}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}Z(z^{\prime})e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert z^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}p(x;z^{\prime})\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}z^{\prime}

It follows from Lemma C.3 that 𝖳𝖵⁡(pR⋆,q)≤16​ϵ{\mathsf{TV}}(p^{\star}_{R},q)\leq 16\epsilon. Combining the above bounds gives 𝖳𝖵⁡(p⋆,q)≤18​ϵ{\mathsf{TV}}(p^{\star},q)\leq 18\epsilon as claimed. ∎

C.2 Technical lemmas

Lemma C.2 (Concentration of χ2\chi^{2}-random variable).

Fix d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} and let Z∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}). Then for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0,

Pr[‖Z‖2>2d+2log⁡(1/ϵ)]≤ϵ.\PR[\left\lVert Z\right\rVert_{2}>2\sqrt{d}+2\sqrt{\log(1/\epsilon)}]\leq\epsilon.
Lemma C.3.

Let f,g:ℝd→ℝ≥0f,g:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be integrable, and let p,q∈Δ⁡(ℝd)p,q\in\Delta(\mathbb{R}^{d}) be defined by p⁡(x)∝f⁡(x)p(x)\propto f(x) and q⁡(x)∝g⁡(x)q(x)\propto g(x). Then

𝖳𝖵⁡(p,q)≤2​∫|f⁡(x)−g⁡(x)|​𝑑x∫f⁡(x)​𝑑x.{\mathsf{TV}}(p,q)\leq\frac{2\int|f(x)-g(x)|\,\mathrm{d}x}{\int f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x}.
Proof.

Set Zf:=∫f⁡(x)​𝑑xZ_{f}:=\int f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x and Zg:=∫g⁡(x)​𝑑xZ_{g}:=\int g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x. Then we have

𝖳𝖵⁡(p,q)\displaystyle{\mathsf{TV}}(p,q) =∫|f⁡(x)Zf−g⁡(x)Zg|​𝑑x\displaystyle=\int\left|\frac{f(x)}{Z_{f}}-\frac{g(x)}{Z_{g}}\right|\,\mathrm{d}x
≤∫|f⁡(x)Zf−g⁡(x)Zf|​𝑑x+∫|g⁡(x)Zf−g⁡(x)Zg|​𝑑x\displaystyle\leq\int\left|\frac{f(x)}{Z_{f}}-\frac{g(x)}{Z_{f}}\right|\,\mathrm{d}x+\int\left|\frac{g(x)}{Z_{f}}-\frac{g(x)}{Z_{g}}\right|\,\mathrm{d}x
≤1Zf​∫|f⁡(x)−g⁡(x)|​𝑑x+|1Zf−1Zg|​∫g⁡(x)​𝑑x\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{Z_{f}}\int|f(x)-g(x)|\,\mathrm{d}x+\left|\frac{1}{Z_{f}}-\frac{1}{Z_{g}}\right|\int g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x
≤1Zf​∫|f⁡(x)−g⁡(x)|​𝑑x+|Zf−Zg|Zf\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{Z_{f}}\int|f(x)-g(x)|\,\mathrm{d}x+\frac{|Z_{f}-Z_{g}|}{Z_{f}}
≤1Zf​∫|f⁡(x)−g⁡(x)|​𝑑x+∫|f⁡(x)−g⁡(x)|​𝑑xZf\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{Z_{f}}\int|f(x)-g(x)|\,\mathrm{d}x+\frac{\int|f(x)-g(x)|\,\mathrm{d}x}{Z_{f}}
=2Zf​∫|f⁡(x)−g⁡(x)|​𝑑x\displaystyle=\frac{2}{Z_{f}}\int|f(x)-g(x)|\,\mathrm{d}x

as claimed. ∎
